lines: A lost path can become a warning if enough people survive telling it.
A wrong turn once taught me more than three careful maps.
Blank space on parchment has a way of <wavy>daring</wavy> people to be foolish.
There is a story from the map table, but it sounds smaller unless you were standing there.
I once followed a map that was right about everything except the bridge being gone.
A traveler brought me a chart with bite marks in the corner. They blamed the road.
One foggy morning the square felt like a foreign country until the bell rang.
I mapped a hill twice because the first version looked too honest to be useful.
A road once vanished under snow and everyone suddenly respected fences.
I saw a trader use the same wrong map for three seasons out of pride.
There was a ravine I marked with extra ink because fear deserved accuracy.
Once a child drew our village with the well bigger than every house. Fair map, really.
I found an old trail by following where grass looked tired.
A cart once broke exactly where my map said nothing interesting happened.
I once drew a coastline while the tide kept editing my work.
The oldest map I trust has a stain where someone survived lunch badly.
A mountain path taught me that up is not a direction, it is an argument.
I mapped a swamp by sound once. Terrible method. Useful fear.
One road led nowhere, then a village grew there and proved everyone wrong.
